title: The restore that doubled a report
outcome: A RESTORE put silver right after a bad load, but gold, fed by a stream, kept the bad rows and the restore added to them.

content.bookmark: RESTORE is a data change: a stream reading the table can see it as new data. And restoring a source never removes what a streaming table already appended downstream.

check.prompt: Which privilege does RESTORE TABLE need?
check.why: Restoring changes the table's data, so it needs MODIFY.

check.prompt: Why can a RESTORE cause duplicates downstream?
options: It is recorded as a data change, so a stream reading the table treats it as new data
It copies the table to a new location
It switches off the transaction log while it runs
check.why: RESTORE is a data-changing operation (dataChange=true). A streaming job reading the table sees it as new data and can produce duplicates downstream.

check.prompt: A streaming table has already appended some rows, and its source is then corrected. What happens to those rows?
options: They are recomputed at the next update, like every other row whose source changed
They stay as they are unless the table is fully refreshed
They are removed when the source is vacuumed
check.why: Rows a streaming table has already appended are not reprocessed; a full refresh clears the table and reprocesses the source.

check.prompt: Which kind of pipeline dataset stays correct when its source updates or deletes rows?
options: A view used only inside the pipeline
check.why: A materialized view is recomputed to match the source's current state, incrementally when possible; it suits sources that update or delete.

caseStudy.setting: A food-delivery company (fictional) keeps orders in silver.orders. A declarative pipeline reads silver.orders as a stream into a gold streaming table, revenue_events, which feeds a revenue dashboard.

events.what: A job is rerun by mistake and appends Wednesday's orders to silver a second time. The pipeline's next update appends them to gold too, and Wednesday's revenue doubles on the dashboard.
An engineer runs RESTORE TABLE silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF the version before the rerun. Silver is correct again.
The dashboard is still wrong. Gold still holds the duplicate orders, and after the restore some appear yet again.

pipeline: Declarative pipeline · streaming read of silver.orders
tasks: Why didn't restoring silver fix gold?
How do they recover, and what should they do next time?

debrief.title: Why gold stayed wrong
text: A streaming table processes each source row once and doesn't reprocess rows it has already appended. Restoring silver changed silver, not the rows gold had already taken.
RESTORE is also recorded as a data change. To a stream reading silver, that commit can look like new data, which is how the restore added to gold instead of cleaning it.

debrief.title: Recovering
text: Run a full refresh of gold.revenue_events: the table is cleared, its checkpoints reset, and the now-correct silver reprocessed. Then check Wednesday's revenue against silver.
Weigh making revenue a materialized view, which is recomputed to match its source, so corrections in silver flow through without a full refresh.

debrief.title: Next time
text: Before restoring a table, find what reads it (lineage shows the downstream tables) and plan the step for each: a full refresh for streaming tables, nothing for materialized views.
Make the load safe to rerun, so a mistaken rerun doesn't duplicate data in the first place.

takeaway: RESTORE is a data change; streams reading the table can duplicate it.
Fixing a source doesn't fix what a streaming table already appended: full refresh it.
Plan the downstream step before you restore.
content.honesty: If you haven't restored a production table, say so, and explain what RESTORE does to downstream streams. If you have, describe how you handled the consumers.

tasks: What should be known about a table before anyone restores it?
What would you ask for in the runbook?

debrief.title: Before restoring
text: Who reads it, and how: as a stream, through a materialized view, or in a report.

debrief.title: Runbook
text: A restore procedure that lists the downstream tables and the step for each one, ending with a check of the figures users see.

sayIt.question: How do you make sure fixing one data problem doesn't create another?
points: Know who depends on the data before changing it.
Use lineage to see the downstream tables.
Plan the downstream steps with the fix.
Check results downstream after the fix.
Keep the procedure written down.

tasks: What do you tell dashboard users?
How do you avoid a second surprise?

debrief.title: Dashboard users
text: Wednesday's revenue is overstated while a correction runs; figures will be right by a stated time.

debrief.title: No second surprise
text: Agree that any repair of a shared table includes the downstream plan and a check of the figures users see.

sayIt.question: A fix didn't fix the dashboard users look at. What do you do?
points: Warn users quickly and say what is affected.
Pause further changes until the plan is clear.
Correct downstream, then check the figures.
Explain what happened in plain terms.
Add downstream checks to the repair procedure.

tasks: How do you run the recovery?

debrief.title: Recovery
text: Full refresh of gold, reconcile Wednesday's revenue against silver, then confirm with the dashboard owner.

debrief.title: Process
text: Restores of shared tables go through a short review that names the downstream tables and their steps; loads are made safe to rerun.

sayIt.question: How do you control risky operational changes without slowing the team down?
points: Keep a lightweight review for operations that affect others.
Write runbooks for common repairs.
Make the safe option the documented one.
Review incidents to improve the runbooks.
Trust the team inside agreed limits.

tasks: Would you change the gold table's design?

debrief.title: Now
text: A full refresh of the gold streaming table from the pipeline, then a reconciliation query comparing gold and silver for Wednesday.

debrief.title: Design
text: If silver is ever corrected in place, a materialized view for revenue is the safer fit. A streaming table suits append-only sources.

sayIt.question: How do you recover a Delta table from a bad write, and what are the side effects?
points: RESTORE TABLE to a version or timestamp; it needs MODIFY and the old files must still exist.
RESTORE is a data change, so streams reading the table can produce duplicates.
Streaming tables don't reprocess rows already appended: full refresh them.
Materialized views are recomputed to match their source.
Check the downstream figures after the repair.
